newsitem.title: INDIA: Resistance trims India stocks surge, end lower.
newsitem.headline: Resistance trims India stocks surge, end lower.

text.p: Shares across India finished lower on Monday as prices met with resistance as it neared a psychological barrier after starting stronger for the seventh straight week, brokers said.
"The market's a bit nervous at 4,400 levels," said Rasesh Maniar, a dealer at brokerage Mukesh Babu Securities Ltd. "We saw some unwinding of positions."
Traders said foreign fund buying, the market's mainstay, was limited to some blue-chip pharmaceutical stocks.
The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index ended 32.37 points, or 0.75 percent, lower at 4,291.45 -- after rising to 4,391.01 early trade.
A government decision at the weekend to divest holdings in four state-run firms including Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd (MTNL) was one reason for selective selling in some counters, traders said.
"The reaction in MTNL is a clear indication," said Antony Sequeira, managing director, at Arcadia Share and Stock Brokers.
MTNL shares fell 31.75 rupees, or 9.96 percent, to 287.0.
In the case of MTNL, a divestment panel has called for the government to sell 47 million shares, and a fresh issue of 60 million shares. The government's holdings will then come down to 52.6 percent.
The government has not set a price for the divestment of each stock and the market reaction was more in anticipation of a rise in availability of shares, traders said.
Analysts expect the market to rebound after undergoing a technical correction propelled by rising inflows from foreign institutional investors (FIIs).
Leading software firm Infosys Technologies Ltd said on Monday its net profit soared 103 percent to 92.2 million rupees in the first quarter ended June 30.
Infosys shares leapt 181 rupees, or 9.03 percent, to 2,185 at the BSE.
India's 15-party United Front government said on Monday it has put off a scheduled meeting of its decision-making body on raising oil prices.

The decision has already been deferred twice as it could not reach a consensus on tackling a huge oil pool deficit -- the money owed to oil companies for selling petroleum products below market prices to support India's subsidy regime.
